```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 120)

# install.packages(c("xgboost", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "here", "knitr"))
library(xgboost)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(knitr)

set.seed(2026)

# ---- switches ---------------------------------------------------------------
data_file  <- "~/Documents/NUTM-STAT-Group-17/Rcode/shared_df_filter.rds"
save_folds <- FALSE   # TRUE writes Rcode/cv_folds_ckd.rds so Isabelle's random forest can reuse identical folds
n_rep      <- 5       # repeats of stratified k-fold CV
k_fold     <- 5
n_threads  <- 2
```

## Aim

Use gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) to ask two questions about CKD in adults aged 35+:

1. Does alcohol intake help predict CKD, and **does sex modify that relationship**?
2. Secondary: does sex modify the **smoking**–CKD relationship?

XGBoost can pick up non-linear effects and interactions that the logistic regression and GAM cannot, so it is used here as a flexible check on those models. All results are **associations**, not causal effects.

## 1. Data

```{r data}
df <- readRDS(data_file)

# Outcome: CKD = 1 if EGFRKDSA stage 1-6, 0 if no indicators of CKD
y <- as.integer(as.character(df$CKD))

# Predictors. Everything is numeric so SHAP values are easy to read.
as01 <- function(f) as.integer(as.character(f))

bev_cols <- c("Low_alcohol_beer", "Mid_strength_beer", "Full_strength_beer",
              "White_wine", "Red_wine", "Low_alcohol_wine",
              "Champagne_sparkling_wine", "Spirits_RTD", "Liqueurs",
              "Spirits", "Fortified_wine", "Cider", "Cocktails")

X <- data.frame(
  male             = as.integer(df$SEX_factor == "Male"),
  AGE              = df$AGE,
  alcohol_quantity = df$alcohol_quantity,   # std drinks/day, last week
  ALC_freq_3       = df$ALC_freq_3,         # ordinal survey code, days with 3+ drinks in past year
  smoker_current   = as.integer(df$smoker_status == "Current smoker"),
  smoker_ex        = as.integer(df$smoker_status == "Ex-smoker"),
  daily_smoke      = as.integer(df$daily_smoke) - 1L  # 0 never, 1 <10y, 2 10-29y, 3 30+y
)
X[bev_cols] <- lapply(df[bev_cols], as01)
X <- as.matrix(X)

alc_vars   <- c("alcohol_quantity", "ALC_freq_3", bev_cols)
smoke_vars <- c("smoker_current", "smoker_ex", "daily_smoke")

# Columns that must NOT be predictors:
#  - eGFR_range: CKD is defined from eGFR/ACR, so it leaks the outcome
#    (every person with eGFR < 60 is coded CKD).
#  - Alcohol_risk / Alcohol_risk_7day: derived from alcohol_quantity.
stopifnot(!any(c("eGFR_range", "Alcohol_risk", "Alcohol_risk_7day") %in% colnames(X)))
stopifnot(!anyNA(X), !anyNA(y), all(y %in% 0:1))

labels <- c(male = "Male sex", AGE = "Age (years)",
            alcohol_quantity = "Alcohol, std drinks/day (last week)",
            ALC_freq_3 = "Days with 3+ drinks (past year, code)",
            smoker_current = "Current smoker", smoker_ex = "Ex-smoker",
            daily_smoke = "Years smoked daily (ordinal)",
            setNames(gsub("_", " ", bev_cols), bev_cols))

sample_tab <- data.frame(
  Group = c("All", "Female", "Male"),
  n     = c(length(y), sum(X[, "male"] == 0), sum(X[, "male"] == 1)),
  CKD   = c(sum(y), sum(y[X[, "male"] == 0]), sum(y[X[, "male"] == 1]))
)
sample_tab$`CKD %` <- round(100 * sample_tab$CKD / sample_tab$n, 1)
kable(sample_tab, caption = "Analysis sample: adults aged 35+ with complete data (shared_df_filter.rds).")
```

**Sample note.** The shared data frame only keeps people with a recorded beverage type, i.e. people who drank in the survey week (only a handful of rows have zero alcohol). There is therefore no non-drinker reference group, and alcohol effects are read *within last-week drinkers*. This should be listed as a limitation.

## 2. Cross-validation set-up

Folds are stratified on CKD × sex so every fold keeps the (small) number of female CKD cases. The same folds are used for every model, so differences between models are not due to different splits.

```{r folds}
make_folds <- function(y, strata, k = 5, reps = 5, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  lapply(seq_len(reps), function(r) {
    fold_id <- integer(length(y))
    for (s in unique(strata)) {
      idx <- which(strata == s)
      fold_id[idx] <- sample(rep_len(seq_len(k), length(idx)))
    }
    lapply(seq_len(k), function(f) which(fold_id == f))  # list of test-index vectors
  })
}

strata  <- paste(y, X[, "male"])
folds   <- make_folds(y, strata, k = k_fold, reps = n_rep)
if (save_folds) saveRDS(folds, here("Rcode", "cv_folds_ckd.rds"))

# Metrics. Accuracy is deliberately not used: predicting "no CKD" for everyone is ~89% accurate.
auc_fn <- function(y, p) {           # Mann-Whitney form of ROC-AUC
  r <- rank(p); n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
ap_fn <- function(y, p) {            # average precision (PR-AUC)
  o <- order(p, decreasing = TRUE); yo <- y[o]
  mean((cumsum(yo) / seq_along(yo))[yo == 1])
}
ll_fn    <- function(y, p) { p <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6); -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p)) }
brier_fn <- function(y, p) mean((y - p)^2)

# Run any model through the repeated CV; returns pooled out-of-fold metrics per repeat.
cv_eval <- function(fit_predict) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(folds), function(r) {
    oof <- numeric(length(y))
    for (te in folds[[r]]) {
      tr <- setdiff(seq_along(y), te)
      oof[te] <- fit_predict(X[tr, , drop = FALSE], y[tr], X[te, , drop = FALSE])
    }
    data.frame(rep = r, AUC = auc_fn(y, oof), PR_AUC = ap_fn(y, oof),
               logloss = ll_fn(y, oof), Brier = brier_fn(y, oof))
  }))
}
```

## 3. Hyper-parameter tuning

Small, shallow trees with strong regularisation, because there are only ~300 CKD cases. Tuning picks the combination with the lowest cross-validated log-loss (using the first repeat's folds). Early stopping picks the number of rounds.

```{r tune}
base_params <- list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
                    subsample = 0.8, nthread = n_threads)

grid <- expand.grid(max_depth = c(2, 3, 4), eta = c(0.03, 0.08),
                    min_child_weight = c(5, 10), colsample_bytree = c(0.6, 0.9))

dall <- xgb.DMatrix(X, label = y)

tune_res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  p  <- c(base_params, as.list(grid[i, ]))
  cv <- xgb.cv(params = p, data = dall, nrounds = 1000, folds = folds[[1]],
               early_stopping_rounds = 40, verbose = 0)
  lg <- as.data.frame(cv$evaluation_log)
  j  <- which.min(lg$test_logloss_mean)
  cbind(grid[i, ], nrounds = lg$iter[j], cv_logloss = lg$test_logloss_mean[j])
}))
tune_res <- tune_res[order(tune_res$cv_logloss), ]

best        <- tune_res[1, ]
best_params <- c(base_params, as.list(best[c("max_depth", "eta", "min_child_weight", "colsample_bytree")]))
best_rounds <- best$nrounds

kable(head(tune_res, 6), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Top 6 of 24 hyper-parameter combinations (5-fold CV log-loss).")
```

Hyper-parameters were chosen on the same data used for the performance estimates below, so the absolute AUC is slightly optimistic. Every model in the comparison uses the same settings, so *comparisons* between models are fair. Nested CV would remove the optimism.

## 4. Predictive performance

```{r perf}
xgb_fit_predict <- function(extra = list(), rounds = best_rounds) {
  function(Xtr, ytr, Xte) {
    p <- c(best_params, extra)
    m <- xgb.train(params = p, data = xgb.DMatrix(Xtr, label = ytr), nrounds = rounds, verbose = 0)
    predict(m, Xte)
  }
}

glm_fit_predict <- function(Xtr, ytr, Xte) {   # logistic regression baseline with the sex x alcohol term
  d  <- as.data.frame(Xtr); d$y <- ytr
  m  <- glm(y ~ male * alcohol_quantity + AGE + smoker_current + smoker_ex + daily_smoke,
            data = d, family = binomial())
  predict(m, newdata = as.data.frame(Xte), type = "response")
}

null_fit_predict <- function(Xtr, ytr, Xte) rep(mean(ytr), nrow(Xte))

spw <- sum(y == 0) / sum(y == 1)

res <- list(
  "Null (prevalence only)"                = cv_eval(null_fit_predict),
  "Logistic regression (sex x alcohol)"   = cv_eval(glm_fit_predict),
  "XGBoost"                               = cv_eval(xgb_fit_predict()),
  "XGBoost + scale_pos_weight"            = cv_eval(xgb_fit_predict(list(scale_pos_weight = spw)))
)

perf <- bind_rows(res, .id = "Model") %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  summarise(across(c(AUC, PR_AUC, logloss, Brier),
                   list(mean = mean, sd = sd), .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"), .groups = "drop")

perf_tab <- perf %>%
  transmute(Model,
            AUC       = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", AUC_mean, AUC_sd),
            `PR-AUC`  = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", PR_AUC_mean, PR_AUC_sd),
            `Log-loss`= sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", logloss_mean, logloss_sd),
            Brier     = sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)", Brier_mean, Brier_sd))
kable(perf_tab, caption = paste0("Out-of-fold performance, mean (SD) over ", n_rep,
      " repeats of stratified ", k_fold, "-fold CV. PR-AUC for a no-skill model equals prevalence (",
      round(mean(y), 3), "). scale_pos_weight re-weights CKD cases; it improves ranking of cases but distorts predicted probabilities, so log-loss and Brier are expected to worsen."))
```

## 5. Does sex modify the alcohol association?

XGBoost has no coefficient to test, so effect modification is assessed by **forbidding** the interaction and checking whether predictions get worse. Using `interaction_constraints`, one model is not allowed to put `male` and any alcohol variable in the same tree branch. If sex really changes how alcohol relates to CKD, blocking that interaction should hurt out-of-fold log-loss.

The same is done for sex × smoking (secondary question).

```{r constraint}
# Groups of features allowed to interact.
block_sets <- function(block) {
  idx0 <- function(v) match(v, colnames(X)) - 1L   # xgboost wants 0-based column indices
  list(idx0(setdiff(colnames(X), "male")), idx0(setdiff(colnames(X), block)))
}

res_alc <- cv_eval(xgb_fit_predict(list(interaction_constraints = block_sets(alc_vars))))
res_smk <- cv_eval(xgb_fit_predict(list(interaction_constraints = block_sets(smoke_vars))))
res_free <- res[["XGBoost"]]

delta <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Block sex x alcohol", "Block sex x smoking"),
  `Mean log-loss increase when blocked` = c(mean(res_alc$logloss - res_free$logloss),
                                            mean(res_smk$logloss - res_free$logloss)),
  `Repeats where blocking was worse` = c(sprintf("%d / %d", sum(res_alc$logloss > res_free$logloss), n_rep),
                                         sprintf("%d / %d", sum(res_smk$logloss > res_free$logloss), n_rep)),
  `Mean AUC change` = c(mean(res_alc$AUC - res_free$AUC), mean(res_smk$AUC - res_free$AUC)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(delta, digits = 5, caption = "Effect of forbidding sex interactions (constrained minus unconstrained, out-of-fold). Positive log-loss increase = the interaction was useful.")
```

```{r constraint-verdict, results='asis'}
d1 <- delta[[2]][1]
cat(if (d1 > 0.001 && sum(res_alc$logloss > res_free$logloss) == n_rep)
      "**Reading:** blocking sex x alcohol consistently worsened out-of-fold log-loss, which supports effect modification by sex."
    else
      "**Reading:** blocking sex x alcohol made little or no difference to out-of-fold log-loss, so XGBoost finds no extra predictive information in a sex-specific alcohol effect. This does not prove there is no interaction (about 300 CKD cases gives limited power) and should be compared with the likelihood-ratio test from the logistic regression.")
```

The repeats share one dataset, so they are not independent replicates. Treat this as descriptive evidence, not a formal hypothesis test.

## 6. What drives the predictions? (SHAP)

SHAP values split each person's predicted CKD log-odds into contributions from each variable. The final model is fitted on all data with the tuned settings.

```{r shap}
final <- xgb.train(best_params, dall, nrounds = best_rounds, verbose = 0)

# SHAP values via xgboost's built-in TreeSHAP (the argument differs between xgboost versions)
attempts <- list(
  function() predict(final, dall, predcontrib = TRUE),
  function() predict(final, X, predcontrib = TRUE),
  function() predict(final, dall, type = "contrib"),
  function() predict(final, X, type = "contrib")
)
S <- NULL
for (f in attempts) {
  out <- tryCatch(as.matrix(f()), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(out) && nrow(out) == nrow(X) && ncol(out) >= ncol(X)) { S <- out; break }
}
if (is.null(S)) stop("No SHAP output. xgboost version: ", packageVersion("xgboost"))
S <- S[, seq_len(ncol(X)), drop = FALSE]   # variables come first; drop the intercept column
colnames(S) <- colnames(X)

imp <- sort(colMeans(abs(S)), decreasing = TRUE)
```

```{r shap-bar, fig.cap="Figure 1. Mean absolute SHAP value per variable (importance on the log-odds scale). XGBoost, n = all adults 35+. Correlated beverage columns share credit, so individual beverage bars understate beverage type as a whole (see Table 4)."}
imp_df <- data.frame(var = names(imp), importance = imp) %>%
  slice_head(n = 12) %>%
  mutate(label = factor(labels[var], levels = rev(labels[var])))
ggplot(imp_df, aes(importance, label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C78A8") +
  labs(x = "Mean |SHAP| (log-odds)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r shap-swarm, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Figure 2. SHAP values per person for the 12 most important variables. Each point is one person; colour is the person's own value of that variable (rank-scaled within variable)."}
top <- names(imp)[1:12]
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(top, function(v) {
  data.frame(var = v, shap = S[, v],
             value = rank(X[, v], ties.method = "average") / length(y))
}))
long$label <- factor(labels[long$var], levels = rev(labels[top]))
set.seed(1)
ggplot(long, aes(shap, label, colour = value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.22, size = 0.7, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#4C78A8", high = "#E45756", name = "Feature value",
                        breaks = c(0.1, 0.9), labels = c("low", "high")) +
  labs(x = "SHAP value (impact on CKD log-odds)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r shap-group}
grp <- list(
  "Age"                         = "AGE",
  "Sex"                         = "male",
  "Alcohol quantity"            = "alcohol_quantity",
  "Alcohol frequency (3+ drinks)" = "ALC_freq_3",
  "Beverage type (13 flags)"    = bev_cols,
  "Smoking (3 variables)"       = smoke_vars
)
grp_tab <- data.frame(Group = names(grp),
                      `Mean |SHAP| (summed)` = sapply(grp, function(v) sum(colMeans(abs(S[, v, drop = FALSE]))))
                      , check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
grp_tab <- grp_tab[order(-grp_tab[[2]]), ]
kable(grp_tab, digits = 4, caption = "Table 4. Grouped SHAP importance. Summing over related columns avoids the dilution that correlated beverage flags cause for single-variable importance.")
```

### Alcohol effect by sex

If sex modifies the alcohol association, the alcohol SHAP curve should differ between males and females.

```{r shap-sex, fig.cap="Figure 3. SHAP contribution of alcohol quantity (last week) to CKD log-odds, by sex. Points are individuals; lines are loess smooths with 95% bands. Separated or diverging lines suggest sex-specific alcohol effects; overlapping lines suggest none. Interpret the right-hand tail cautiously: few people drink heavily."}
sh <- data.frame(alcohol = X[, "alcohol_quantity"], shap = S[, "alcohol_quantity"],
                 Sex = factor(ifelse(X[, "male"] == 1, "Male", "Female")))
ggplot(sh, aes(alcohol, shap, colour = Sex, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.9, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.15) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, quantile(sh$alcohol, 0.98))) +
  labs(x = "Alcohol, standard drinks per day (last week)",
       y = "SHAP value for alcohol quantity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 7. Assumptions and limitations

- **Alcohol exposure window.** Alcohol is recorded for the survey week only, while CKD develops over years. Binge drinking and regular light drinking are not distinguished by the weekly quantity.
- **Reverse causation.** People diagnosed with CKD often cut back on drinking, which can make drinkers look protected.
- **Sample.** Only last-week drinkers aged 35+ with complete data are included; there is no non-drinker reference group.
- **Leakage avoided.** `eGFR_range` (which defines CKD) and the risk categories derived from alcohol quantity were excluded from the predictors.
- **Importance with correlated predictors.** Beverage-type flags overlap with total quantity, so single-variable importance is diluted; grouped importance (Table 4) is more reliable.
- **Small numbers.** About 313 CKD cases (113 female, 200 male) limit power to detect interactions.
- **Association only.** Neither SHAP values nor the constraint test establish causation.
- **Tuning optimism.** Hyper-parameters were tuned on the same data as the performance estimates; nested CV would remove this.
